title: Scaling Memcache: caching billions of reads a second
dek: In 2013 the largest social network described how it turned memcached, a simple in-memory key-value cache, into a system handling billions of requests a second for over a billion users. The paper is a catalogue of the problems every big cache meets: stale data, thundering herds, failed servers and keeping several regions in step.

items: A look-aside cache: read from the cache; on a miss read the database and fill the cache; on a write update the database and delete the key. Deletes are safe to repeat, updates are not.
Leases fix two classic bugs at once: a stale value written over a fresh one, and a thousand requests hitting the database when a popular key is deleted.
At scale the hard parts are around the cache: one page needs hundreds of keys, failed servers must not push load onto the database, and deletes must reach every copy in every region.

body.x: The paper: "Scaling Memcache at Facebook" by Rajesh Nishtala and twelve co-authors, NSDI 2013.

A social feed is read far more than it is written, and one page is built from hundreds of small pieces: names, photos, likes, comments. Serving every piece from databases was impossible at that scale. The authors put memcached, a plain in-memory key-value server, in front of the databases and then spent years on the problems that appear once the cache holds trillions of items and answers billions of requests a second.
Zotato's restaurant page is the same shape: the menu, ratings, photos, offers and delivery times, fetched as dozens of keys for every visitor.

items: Read: ask the cache; on a miss, read the database and put the value in the cache.
Write: update the database, then delete the key from the cache. The next read refills it.
Deleting rather than updating the cache is deliberate: deleting twice is harmless, while two updates that arrive in the wrong order leave the wrong value behind.

body.x: Leases: one miss, not a thousand

body.cap: A lease is a token the cache hands out on a miss. Only the holder may fill the key, and the cache hands out at most one token per key every 10 seconds, so a popular key costs the database one read instead of a thousand.

body.x: Leases also fix stale sets. Suppose two readers miss, one reads the old menu, a write deletes the key, and the slow reader then writes the old menu back. With leases the delete cancels the outstanding token, so the late write is refused and the stale menu never lands.

body.cap: The user who made the change sees it at once, because their web server deletes the key locally. Everyone else's cache learns of it from the database's own commit log, the one place every committed write is recorded.

items: Hundreds of keys per page: requests are batched and sent in parallel, and a window limits how many are in flight so replies don't overflow switch buffers.
Failed servers: about 1% of servers form a gutter pool that briefly takes over a dead server's keys, so its load doesn't land on the database.
New clusters warm up by reading from a warm cluster's cache instead of the database.
Across regions, writes go to the primary region's database and replicate; a remote marker sends a user's next read to the primary until replication catches up, so they don't see their old data.

body.x: The system is eventually consistent by design: a reader can see a stale value for a short time, and the authors accept that for a social feed. Every mechanism in the paper narrows the window or limits the damage. None of it makes the cache strongly consistent with the database.

items: Describe the look-aside pattern exactly, including 'write: update the database, then delete the key'. Interviewers listen for the delete.
Name the thundering herd and the fix: leases or a lock per key, so one request refills and the rest wait. Add a little random jitter to expiry times so many keys don't expire together.
Say what happens when a cache server dies: a spare pool or consistent hashing, so the database doesn't take the full load.
Say how invalidation reaches other regions (from the database's change log) and how a user reads their own writes.
See the Caches component for the patterns, and the News feed and Restaurants near me problems for where they apply.

body.label: Go deeper: the numbers that made leases worth it

body.x: The paper reports that for one workload, leases cut the database's peak query rate from 17,000 to 1,300 a second. Requests that are told to wait usually find the value filled within milliseconds. For data where slightly old is fine, the cache can even hand a waiting request the just-deleted value instead of making it wait at all.
